lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Flush's ecstatic welcome home captures an early, vivid domestic moment.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert's confession about shortening visits to take Ba's hand is an intimate private gesture.
The armchair cushion is their private shorthand for a hidden thought.

lines.text: ‘Comfort me with apples, for I am sick of love!’
lines.note: Robert's apple parable turns a homely image into counsel about not delaying.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Elizabeth's shock at losing Flush shows the depth of her attachment.

lines.text: Another may be that I may have an opportunity of ‘forgiving’ you, which I have not had yet.
lines.note: Elizabeth's Pisa line playfully promises forgiveness, calling back to Robert's earlier counsel.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: Elizabeth's 'I am your Flush' turns the dog-stealer dispute into mutual tenderness.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush found and lying on the sofa marks the happy resolution of the ordeal.

lines.text: What a glorious dream; through nearly two years—without a single interval of blankness,—much less, bitter waking!
lines.note: Robert's two-year dream frames their secret courtship as uninterrupted wonder.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: Elizabeth's 'one will which is yours' is a decisive turning point.

lines.text: When we drove past that church again, I and my sisters, there was a cloud before my eyes.
lines.note: The cloud before Elizabeth's eyes on passing the church captures the weight of the wedding day.

lines.text: I did hate so, to have to take off the ring!
lines.note: Her hatred of removing the ring is a small, intimate post-wedding detail.

lines.text: Bless you, my very own, only Ba—my pride, and joy, and utter comfort.
lines.note: Robert's 'pride, and joy, and utter comfort' seals his gratitude after the marriage.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's 'By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only' looks ahead to their departure.
